summary:
SPACE HEALTH is an intelligent platform that assists astronauts in monitoring health markers, understanding changes within their own bodies, and making decisions through contextualized guidance and practical action guides during space missions.

In isolated environments, astronauts need to identify changes in their health without necessarily possessing medical expertise or the ability to interpret vast amounts of data. To address this challenge, the platform transforms complex information into a visual, interactive, and human-centered experience.

Its key feature is the "Organ Race"—a playful experience in which organs come to life as characters that move and react to shifts in health indicators, making the monitoring process more intuitive and engaging. This is complemented by an interactive body avatar, which allows users to explore different parts of the body, and a conversational assistant that clarifies information and provides practical guidance—without replacing professional medical assessment.

Beyond simply monitoring data, SPACE HEALTH aims to reduce cognitive overload, foster autonomy, make daily routines feel lighter and more welcoming, and mitigate the emotional impact of loneliness and isolation in space.
details:
SPACE HEALTH is an intelligent platform for managing astronaut health, designed to transform health monitoring into a playful, interactive, and engaging experience. By utilizing visual elements, characters, and interactive features, it turns complex medical data and charts into a more accessible format, helping users better understand their own bodies and supporting decision-making during space missions.

How it works: The platform organizes test data, physiological indicators, and health records into two primary environments: "Health" and "Mission." In the Health section, the core experience is the "Organ Race": the heart, lungs, brain, kidneys, and liver come to life as expressive 3D characters, each on its own track. Their movements and reactions reflect the status of the associated health indicators, making monitoring more intuitive and enjoyable—without turning it into a medical competition between the organs. This is complemented by an interactive body avatar, which allows users to explore different parts of the body and access specific information, as well as a "Mission Companion"—a conversational assistant that provides explanations regarding health indicators, medical tests, and guidance in plain, accessible language, helping astronauts understand their data and determine their next steps.

The Mission environment also employs a visual, game-like approach to organize tasks, medical tests, and equipment, using colorful maps and interactive journeys to track milestones, pending items, and overall progress. This visual structure helps astronauts better perceive the passage of time, making their mission routine easier to grasp and follow day by day. On Earth, mission control professionals can monitor incoming data, analyze alerts, and review guidance, ensuring continued human oversight.

Technology and data: The interface was developed using TypeScript and React, while the backend is built with Python 3, its standard library, SQLite databases, and HTTP APIs. It integrates real-world data from the OSD-575 study—available in the NASA Open Science Data Repository and pertaining to the Inspiration4 mission—comprising 531 records, four crew members, 19 blood analytes, and seven collection time points. The system features the processing of test results in PDF, XLSX, CSV, and text formats, a deterministic rules engine, comparisons against individual baselines, a protocol assistant with local search capabilities, and synchronization between onboard and Earth-based databases—even in scenarios where communication is interrupted.

Benefits and impact: the system aims to reduce cognitive load, facilitate the identification of changes, foster autonomy, and support more informed decision-making, all while complementing—rather than replacing—healthcare professionals. The proposal also seeks to make the care routine more welcoming, engaging, and human-centered, helping to mitigate the emotional effects of loneliness and isolation in space.

Creativity and key considerations: the primary innovation lies in using a playful, game-like approach to help astronauts engage with their own health, replacing the traditional experience of complex medical dashboards with a narrative, visual, and participatory interaction. Expressive anatomical characters, body visualization, and conversational assistance make health monitoring more engaging without compromising the seriousness of the information. The project accounts for the limitations of space communication, the necessity for offline functionality, data clarity and traceability, security, and the essential role of professional oversight. It is an engineering prototype designed for demonstration purposes and is not a certified medical device.
